claims.text: Under tribo-corrosion, coupled degradation in high-entropy alloys is primarily governed by mechanical disruption of the passive surface film.
High shear stresses during sliding disrupt the passive surface film.
Mechanical loading during sliding induces localized grain refinement.
Mechanically induced grain refinement redistributes passive-film-forming elements such as Cr.
Redistribution of protective elements compromises passive-film integrity.
Passive-film disruption and grain refinement synergistically accelerate both wear and corrosion.
A coarse-grained, single-phase Cantor-type HEA can provide an initial state with an intact, chemically stable passive film.
Sliding wear produces high strain rates that cause local plastic deformation and grain refinement.
Processing-induced stresses and grain refinement can reduce the corrosion resistance of Cantor-type HEAs.
A compromised passive film accelerates localized corrosion.
Corroded regions become more susceptible to subsequent mechanical damage, creating a positive wear-corrosion feedback cycle.
Tribo-corrosion will produce greater total degradation than either static corrosion or wear in an inert environment.
Tribo-corrosion will increase the corrosion rate because of passive-film breakdown.
Tribo-corrosion will increase the wear rate because of surface microstructural alteration.
Wear tracks should contain refined-grain zones spatially coincident with disrupted passive layers.
In the static-corrosion baseline, the passive film remains intact.
A stable dense microstructure and strong mechanical properties can improve tribo-corrosion resistance in an HEA coating.
A robust dense oxide layer may suppress the proposed passive-film-disruption mechanism.
Heat treatment that relieves residual stress and homogenizes the grain structure restores corrosion resistance in a processed Cantor alloy.
Stress-relieved and grain-homogenized HEAs may fall outside the regime in which the proposed tribo-corrosion mechanism operates.
